question: Can grokking be explained as stochastic-gradient noise driving escape from deliberately prepared lower-rank metastable phases in an L2-regularized deep linear network, with escape time following an Arrhenius law in batch size divided by learning rate?

key_findings.claim: Under balanced initialization and aligned input-output covariances, the depth-three linear network decomposes into independent singular modes with an explicit nonconvex scalar objective.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reduces each mode to one half (lambda - eta)^2 plus beta L/2 times lambda^(2/L), so stationarity obeys lambda - eta + beta lambda^(2/L - 1) = 0.

anchors.section: Section 2.1, L2 phase transitions and mode decomposition

key_findings.claim: For depth at least three, the scalar landscape can contain zero, a saddle, and a positive local minimum, with a saddle-node threshold in weight decay and one rank-changing transition per singular mode.
key_findings.evidence: The stationary-point and phase-diagram analysis derives the critical beta at which the nonzero minimum and saddle merge and interprets occupied modes as the network's effective rank.

anchors.section: Appendices C-D.1, saddle-node and critical regularization

key_findings.claim: The paper's phases are rank-indexed local minima and beta-driven saddle-node bifurcations, not thermodynamic phases established through a model-size limit.
key_findings.evidence: The analytic control parameter is L2 regularization beta and the experiment uses one depth-three width-10 network. No width or sample-size scaling tests a singular limit; the later stochastic event is a first-passage escape between finite-dimensional basins.

key_findings.claim: The formal landscape result establishes possible metastable rank states, but it does not prove the stochastic escape law or establish that ordinary Transformer grokking occupies those states.
key_findings.evidence: The analytic derivation concerns aligned deep-linear singular modes and stationary points; Kramers scaling, effective temperature, and the grokking interpretation are supplied as approximations and experiments rather than a theorem covering SGD or nonlinear models.

key_findings.claim: The main Gaussian experiment intentionally creates rank-zero and rank-one checkpoints by annealing at high regularization before switching to the target training regime.
key_findings.evidence: A depth-three width-10 network with two output modes is trained on 512 Gaussian samples; the target run uses beta = 0.32, learning rate 0.08, batch size 64, and 20,000 epochs, with 50 seeds per prepared initialization.

key_findings.claim: Prepared rank controls produce long, sequential plateaus, whereas the standard random initialization reaches its final solution quickly and does not exhibit the claimed trapping mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 reports convergence in roughly 10 epochs from random initialization, escape from rank one near 5,500 epochs, and two successive escapes from rank zero extending beyond 10,000 epochs.

key_findings.claim: The paper's own standard-initialization result makes engineered basin occupancy a necessary condition for its headline delay in the tested Gaussian setting.
key_findings.evidence: The roughly three-order difference between standard and trapped trajectories is induced by the checkpoint preparation, not observed as a common distribution over ordinary random seeds; no frequency of naturally entering the lower-rank basins is estimated.

key_findings.claim: The sparse-sample experiment reproduces delayed alignment of test and training performance without an intervening memorization solution.
key_findings.evidence: The model is trained on 25 examples sampled from a pool of 5,000 and tested on 10,000, with teacher singular values 0.9 and 0.8, beta = 0.0025, learning rate 0.1, batch size 64, and a rank-one start; after about 1,500 epochs, test performance approaches training performance, while stochastic linear regression prevents either loss from becoming zero.

key_findings.claim: The sparse experiment does not specify a minibatch-noise source: it declares only 25 training examples but batch size 64.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A states N_train = 25 and B = 64 without describing sampling with replacement. A standard without-replacement loader would therefore use one 25-example full batch, not a 64-example minibatch, so this run cannot be reproduced as evidence for noise-activated SGD escape from the stated protocol. Sampling 64 examples with replacement could restore noise, but that materially different protocol is not reported.

key_findings.claim: Calling the sparse experiment canonical grokking broadens the phenomenon beyond its usual memorization-then-generalization definition.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly argue that memorization is unnecessary and acknowledge that the mechanisms may differ; the model is linear, deliberately rank-one initialized, and never attains zero training error before delayed test improvement.

key_findings.claim: The learning-rate sweep is reported as strong Arrhenius evidence: log mean escape time is approximately linear in inverse effective temperature with R-squared 0.991.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 fits the retained low-temperature points, uses a scalar loss barrier near 0.003, and reports an effective fitted barrier of 0.15 +/- 0.05, attributing the roughly fifty-fold difference to entropic curvature effects.

key_findings.claim: The paper's determinant correction does not algebraically explain the roughly fifty-fold fitted barrier: Equation 12 has the opposite sign from the logarithm of its own Equation 11.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 11 writes mean escape time as a curvature prefactor proportional to sqrt(product |omega_sad| / product omega_min) times exp(Delta E / T). Its logarithm therefore adds +(1/2) sum log(omega_sad / omega_min) to the intercept. Equation 12 instead defines Delta E_eff = Delta E - (T/2) sum log(omega_sad / omega_min) and then uses omega_min much greater than omega_sad to increase the barrier, the opposite sign from Equation 11. Even with the sign repaired, a temperature-independent Hessian determinant changes the intercept, not the slope identified as 0.15; no Hessian measurements or temperature dependence establish the claimed correction.

key_findings.claim: The paper does not independently test the claimed effective-temperature law T_eff proportional to learning rate divided by batch size.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A declares five learning rates at fixed batch size 64, each averaged over 50 trials. Batch size is never varied at fixed learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio, so discretization and deterministic learning-rate effects are confounded with noise scale.

key_findings.claim: The documented sweep settings do not match the plotted fit-point count, and the highest-temperature observations are excluded without a reproducible selection rule.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A lists learning rates {5e-4, 1e-3, 2e-3, 3e-3, 5e-3}, but Figure 2b visibly contains about eight retained red markers plus two gray excluded markers; neither the additional settings nor a preregistered exclusion threshold is specified.

key_findings.claim: A primary theoretical comparator predicts non-Arrhenius, power-law escape for multiplicative SGD noise on mean-square loss, directly challenging the fitted linear-loss-barrier interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: The paper mentions Mori et al. only in Appendix F and asserts that it does not change the learning-rate relationship, but it does not test log-loss barriers, Hessian outlier dependence, curvature prefactors, or fit comparison against the power-law theory.

key_findings.claim: Several internal numerical labels conflict with the surrounding method and figures.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1's caption gives beta = 0.03 while the main text and Appendix A give 0.32. Appendix B calls the phase-boundary MSE changes drops although the plotted curve jumps upward, and its beta-critical labels and ordering disagree with eta_1 = 0.9, eta_2 = 0.8, the derived formula, and Figure 4.

key_findings.claim: The headline statement that the number of metastable states equals the number of learnable features is not the state count of the paper's separable objective.
key_findings.evidence: Below all mode thresholds, each decoupled scalar mode has both a zero and a positive local minimum. Their Cartesian products give up to 2^d local-minimum configurations (four for the two-mode example: rank zero, either of two rank-one occupancies, and rank two), while an ordered continuation path has d transitions and d+1 rank phases. The paper conflates modes or transition events with full-network metastable states when it says there is one state per feature.

key_findings.claim: The stated 50-seed replication does not by itself make the escape-time estimator auditable.
key_findings.evidence: The escape threshold is set at a midpoint, but uncertainty construction, censoring of runs that fail to escape, raw escape-time distributions, and the consequences of high-temperature exclusions are not reported.

key_findings.claim: Generalization to nonlinear networks is a research proposal rather than evidence in this paper.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix G discusses possible singular-mode or low-rank analogues and cites prior nonlinear grokking work, but all reported interventions and escape fits use linear networks.

method.core_idea: Construct analytically tractable rank-indexed local minima in an L2-regularized deep linear network, prepare the optimizer inside selected basins, and interpret delayed rank acquisition as noise-driven metastable escape.
method.mechanism: Aligned balanced dynamics reduce training to independent singular modes. L2 regularization creates zero and nonzero minima separated by saddles; minibatch SGD is approximated as Langevin dynamics with temperature proportional to learning rate divided by batch size, yielding an Arrhenius escape-time prediction.
assumptions: Balanced initialization and aligned covariance preserve independent singular-mode dynamics.
The discrete, multiplicative noise of minibatch SGD can be represented by a scalar additive effective temperature proportional to learning rate divided by batch size.
The sparse B=64 run retains a stochastic minibatch-noise source despite having only 25 training examples, although replacement sampling is not specified.
Prepared lower-rank checkpoints represent metastable phases encountered in ordinary grokking runs.
A scalar loss barrier plus an unmeasured entropic correction suffices to interpret the escape-time slope.
Delayed generalization without prior zero training error is mechanistically comparable to canonical grokking.

techniques.role: Reduces the balanced aligned deep-linear objective to independent scalar mode landscapes.
Anneals at high regularization to create controlled rank-zero and rank-one initial states.
Measures first-passage time across a midpoint threshold over repeated SGD runs.
Varies learning rate at fixed batch size and fits an Arrhenius-style log-time relation.

evaluations.setting: Depth-three Gaussian linear regression with standard, rank-one, and rank-zero starts (pp. 3-4); setup details (p. 9)
evaluations.metric: Mode singular values, loss, and time to rank transition
evaluations.result: Figure 1 reports that standard initialization converges near 10 epochs, rank one escapes near 5,500, and rank zero undergoes two sequential transitions beyond 10,000 epochs (pp. 3-4).
evaluations.baseline: Standard random initialization under the same target optimizer settings

evaluations.setting: Sparse 25-example linear teacher-student task (p. 4); setup details (pp. 9-10)
evaluations.metric: Training and test loss over epochs
evaluations.result: A prepared rank-one state shows delayed second-mode acquisition near 1,500 epochs, after which test loss approaches training loss without a prior memorization plateau at zero error; the declared B=64 exceeds N_train=25 and the sampler is unspecified (p. 4); setup details appear on pp. 9-10.
evaluations.baseline: The earlier one-mode plateau in the same trajectory

evaluations.setting: Learning-rate sweep at batch size 64, nominally 50 trials per setting (pp. 4-5); declared sweep details (p. 9)
evaluations.metric: Mean escape time and linear fit of log escape time
evaluations.result: The retained points yield R-squared 0.991 and a fitted effective barrier 0.15 +/- 0.05, but the plotted and declared sweep counts differ, high-temperature points are excluded, and Appendix F's determinant-sign algebra cannot explain the slope (p. 5); the inconsistent derivation is on p. 12.
evaluations.baseline: Arrhenius line fit; no power-law or multiplicative-noise model comparison

evaluations.setting: Analytic regularization phase diagrams for two singular modes (pp. 10-12)
evaluations.metric: Stationary points, loss branches, and critical beta
evaluations.result: The scalar theory predicts sequential disappearance or selection of rank states, though appendix labels conflict with the formula and plotted ordering, and the separable objective has more full-network minima than the stated one-state-per-feature count (pp. 10-12).
evaluations.baseline: Numerical minimization of the reduced scalar objectives

limitations: Author-stated: all direct evidence is linear, and extension to nonlinear networks is speculative.
Author-stated: the sparse task need not memorize, so it may differ from canonical grokking.
Reviewer inference: the long plateaus require deliberately engineered metastable initializations; their prevalence under standard initialization is not measured.
Reviewer inference: batch size is not swept, so T_eff proportional to learning-rate-over-batch-size is not independently tested.
Reviewer inference: the fit omits high-temperature points, contains more markers than declared settings, and lacks alternative escape-law comparison.
Reviewer inference: the sparse run declares B=64 for only 25 training samples without specifying replacement sampling, so its stochastic-noise protocol is indeterminate.

Contradiction audit: Equation 12 reverses the determinant sign implied by Equation 11; a temperature-independent curvature prefactor belongs to the intercept and cannot by itself explain the fitted barrier slope.
Contradiction audit: independent mode bistability yields combinatorial product minima (up to 2^d), not literally one full-network metastable state per feature.
Reviewer inference: internal beta and critical-point inconsistencies obstruct exact reproduction.
Reviewer inference: censoring, uncertainty definitions, and raw seed-level escape times are not reported.
failure_modes: Ordinary initialization can bypass the metastable rank state and remove the delayed transition entirely.
Changing learning rate can alter deterministic discretization and basin stability, invalidating a pure noise-temperature interpretation.
Multiplicative SGD noise can produce a power-law governed by log-loss barriers rather than the assumed Arrhenius law.
A midpoint escape threshold can bias times when trajectories recross, fail to escape within budget, or transition gradually.
Treating a Kramers curvature prefactor as a larger slope can manufacture an apparent effective barrier, especially when its algebraic sign and temperature dependence are not checked.
When batch size exceeds dataset size, an unspecified loader may silently become full-batch or sample with replacement, changing whether the proposed escape noise exists.
A linear low-rank transition can improve test loss without reproducing memorization, nonlinear circuit formation, or Transformer grokking.
reusable_insights: Basin preparation is a powerful causal tool, but natural basin occupancy must be measured separately from what a prepared state can do.
Effective-temperature claims require factorial learning-rate and batch-size sweeps with matched continuous-time drift, not a one-axis learning-rate sweep.
Escape studies should publish uncensored first-passage distributions and compare Arrhenius, power-law, and nonstationary hazard models under fixed inclusion rules.
Mode-wise deep-linear landscapes provide clean theorem-to-experiment alignment only within their balance and covariance assumptions.
Delayed test improvement should be labeled grokking-like when training never first memorizes the sample.

A claimed free-energy correction should be derived directly from the reported rate equation: temperature-independent determinants change an Arrhenius intercept, while slope changes require measured temperature dependence.
open_questions: How often do standard nonlinear or Transformer runs enter rank-deficient metastable basins without checkpoint engineering?
Do escape times collapse when learning rate and batch size are co-varied at fixed noise scale while deterministic step size is separately controlled?
Does a multiplicative-noise power-law model outperform the reported Arrhenius fit on preregistered, unfiltered seed-level data?
Can rank-state interventions predict and change generalization on canonical modular arithmetic while preserving matched training loss?
After correcting the sign in Equation 12, do measured Hessian determinants vary with temperature strongly enough to alter the Arrhenius slope rather than only its intercept?
Was the 25-example run sampled with replacement, and does its delayed transition persist under an explicit factorial batch-size protocol?

competitive_landscape.title: Phase Transitions between Accuracy Regimes in L2 regularized Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This earlier work already studies L2-induced accuracy phases, local minima, hysteresis, and grokking-like jumps; the present paper's narrower addition is controlled deep-linear rank metastability and a proposed SGD escape-time law.

competitive_landscape.title: Power-law escape rate of SGD
competitive_landscape.difference: Mori et al. derive that multiplicative SGD noise for mean-square loss yields escape governed by a log-loss barrier and power-law behavior, contrary to a linear-loss Arrhenius borrowing; the present paper does not fit or falsify that alternative.

competitive_landscape.title: Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Saxe et al. already derive independent singular-mode plateaus and rapid stage-like learning under aligned balanced conditions; the present paper adds L2-created local minima and stochastic checkpoint escape.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit bias of SGD in $L_{2}$-regularized linear DNNs: One-way jumps from high to low rank
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang and Jacot prove stochastic accessibility and absorbing low-rank sets for L2-regularized linear DNNs, with one-way high-to-low rank jumps; the present experiment emphasizes prepared low-to-high mode acquisition and an Arrhenius timing interpretation.

competitive_landscape.title: Phase transitions reveal hierarchical structure in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This work studies sequential phase transitions as hierarchical feature structure is acquired in deep networks; the present paper instead assigns sequential steps to independent singular-mode escape in a prepared linear landscape.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking in Linear Estimators -- A Solvable Model that Groks without Understanding
competitive_landscape.difference: Levi et al. derive delayed accuracy in linear estimators and show that thresholded accuracy can create apparent grokking without a representational phase change; the present paper uses loss and rank transitions but does not rule out metric-induced sharpness in its grokking framing.

competitive_landscape.title: Dichotomy of Early and Late Phase Implicit Biases Can Provably Induce Grokking
competitive_landscape.difference: This theory explains grokking through a change from early optimization bias to late regularized bias without requiring noise-driven barrier escape; the present paper does not compare basin residence against that deterministic two-phase account.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking as a First Order Phase Transition in Two Layer Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This work attributes abrupt generalization to competition between memorizing and generalizing solutions in a tractable nonlinear setting; the present paper attributes timing to stochastic escape among rank states and does not include a memorizing solution in its sparse demonstration.

competitive_landscape.title: Is Grokking a Computational Glass Relaxation?
competitive_landscape.difference: The computational-glass account studies rugged nonlinear solutions and reports that grokking need not follow a simple entropy-barrier picture; the present paper's basin is an engineered low-rank linear minimum with an unmeasured entropic correction.

competitive_landscape.title: Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: Mechanistic progress measures reveal gradual Fourier-circuit formation before the accuracy jump in modular addition; the present model instead produces abrupt independent mode escapes and supplies no circuit-level nonlinear evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
competitive_landscape.difference: The canonical phenomenon requires fitting a small algorithmic training set long before test generalization; the present sparse linear experiment deliberately omits that memorization stage and should therefore be treated as grokking-like rather than a direct reproduction.

competitive_landscape.title: Low-Dimensional and Transversely Curved Optimization Dynamics in Grokking
competitive_landscape.difference: This Transformer study reports low-dimensional confinement and transverse-curvature growth before modular-arithmetic grokking, with interventions showing orthogonal motion is necessary but boosted curvature is insufficient. It supplies nonlinear metastable-regime evidence absent here, but does not establish an Arrhenius SGD escape law or the prepared deep-linear rank mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: A Stochastic--Geometric Theory of Scaling Laws in Grokking
competitive_landscape.relationship: current stochastic escape and scaling competitor
competitive_landscape.difference: This post-target theory models Adam with weight-shrinkage as escape from a shell-core memorization geometry and derives scaling in learning rate, batch size, and L2 regularization. Its broader factorial scaling claims are an exact current comparison for the present paper's fixed-batch learning-rate line, though its optimizer, geometry, and nonlinear experiments differ.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that grokking is noise-driven escape from metastable phases, with an analytically controlled deep-linear system exhibiting rank plateaus, sequential transitions, and Arrhenius escape scaling in effective SGD temperature.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The scalar mode landscape rigorously shows possible rank-indexed local minima under restrictive aligned balanced assumptions. Prepared checkpoints produce long plateaus over 50 runs, and a selected learning-rate regime gives a high-R-squared line. However, batch size is fixed in that sweep, Figure 2 has more points than the five declared settings, the 25-example run declares B=64 without a sampler, Equation 12 reverses its own Kramers determinant sign, and nonlinear or naturally initialized grokking is not demonstrated.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The credible novelty is a clean experimental construction of low-rank metastable checkpoints and delayed mode acquisition in an L2 deep-linear model. Broad explanatory priority is limited by earlier L2 phase, rank-jump, deep-linear plateau, implicit-bias, glass, nonlinear-geometry, and current stochastic-scaling accounts. The headline Arrhenius mechanism is not verified: a primary theory predicts power-law multiplicative-noise escape, only learning rate is swept, points are selectively excluded, the determinant correction cannot explain the fitted slope as written, the sparse noise protocol is indeterminate, and standard initialization bypasses trapping.

verification.passage_check: Independently re-read all 13 pages of the exact official arXiv:2606.17120v1 PDF (2026-06-15), including every equation, all four figures, the complete experimental setup, phase and bifurcation diagrams, critical-strength derivation, barrier calculation, Kramers--Langer appendix, multiplicative-noise discussion, and nonlinear extrapolation. Every finding and anchor was checked against extracted text and rendered pages; the pass added the B>N_train protocol defect, corrected appendix anchors, derived the Equation 11-to-12 sign contradiction, and audited the full product-state count.
verification.competitor_check: Re-searched official primary literature and checked exact current arXiv records and revision dates on 2026-08-23 for all 13 competitors: 2505.06597v2, 2105.09557v2, 1312.6120v3, 2305.16038v2, 2512.11866v1, 2310.16441v1, 2311.18817v2, 2310.03789v3, 2505.11411v5, 2301.05217v3, 2201.02177v1, 2602.16746v3, and 2606.30388v3. Titles, abstracts, mechanism overlap, contradictory evidence, current versions, source dates, and version-specific URLs were verified; the target was excluded.

reviewer_notes: Secondary verification used the byte-identical official current v1 PDF and covered all 13 pages through Appendices A-G. PDF/text hashes, page count, and locator exactly match fulltext_index.jsonl. Rendered inspection confirms the Figure 1 beta conflict and Figure 2 point-count mismatch. Direct algebra confirms beta_c(eta=0.9) is about 0.411 and beta_c(eta=0.8) about 0.351, exposing the swapped appendix indices; Equation 12 also has the wrong determinant sign relative to Equation 11. No code, raw seed-level times, sampler definition, censoring records, or Hessian spectra are available, so empirical reruns and the authors' intended B=64 sparse sampling remain unresolved.
